WRITTEN ANSWERS TO STARRED QUESTIONS 
Right to land and shelter 
*61. SHRI RAVULA CHANDRA SEKAR REDDY: Will the Minister of HOUSING 
AND URBAN POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have any proposal to provide shelter to the poor and 
landless people by enacting a law like right to land and right to shelter; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether it is a fact that poor people are agitating for land in Andhra Pradesh; 
(e) if so, the details thereof; 
(f) whether some people have died due to police action during the recent agitation;
  
(g) if so, the details thereof; and 
(h) the steps Government are taking to give land and house to the weaker and poorer 
sections of the society, especially in Andhra Pradesh? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE OF THE MINISTRY OF HOUSING AND URBAN 
POVERTY ALLEVIATION (KUMARI SELJA): (a) to (c) There is no proposal with the 
Central Government to enact any law with regard to right to land or right to shelter, as 
the subject comes under the purview of State Governments. However, State 
Governments are requested from time to time to ensure distribution of ceiling surp lus 
land, Government Wasteland and Bhoodan land among eligible  rural poor. The 
Central Government has also been providing funds to the State Governments under the 
Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission (JNNURM) to provide for shelter 
and basic services and other related civic  amenities to urban poor. 
(d) and (e) Andhra Pradesh Government has reported that certain activists have 
launched an agitation on land issue. The Government of Andhra Pradesh had constituted 
a Committee under the Chairmanship o f the Minister for Municipal Administration and 
Urban Development to assess overall implementation of land distribution programme of 
the Government, to suggest measures for their effective implementation, required 
amendments to the Act/Rules for improved e nforcement of land related legislations and 
suggest measures for removal of obstacles in their implementation. 
(f) and (g) Andhra Pradesh Government has reported that there had been a call for 
Rasta Roko at several places in the State including Khammam Dis trict on 28.7.2007 
during the Bandh call given by the activists. There was confrontation between police 
and the agitators as a result of which Police had to open fire on the agitators causing 
death of 6 persons and injury to 8 civilians.  Later one person d ied in the hospital, 
while receiving treatment. 13 Police personnel were also injured due to the agitation. 
The Andhra Pradesh Government has appointed Justice Shri I. Panduranga Rao,  

4        Written Answers  to [RAJYA SABHA] Starred Questions 
Retired Judge. High Court of Andhra Pradesh, as Commissioner of Inquiry to inquire 
into the incident. 
(h) As per information received from various States and UTs 50.34 lacs acres of 
ceiling surplus land, 153.22 lacs acres of Government wasteland and 16.57 lacs acres  of 
Bhoodan land has been distributed among rural poor. These include 5.93 lacs acres of 
ceiling  surplus land 43.93  lacs  acres of Government wasteland 1.10 lacs acres of 
Bhoodan land distributed in the State of Andhra Pradesh. 
The Government under the Jawa harlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission 
(JNNURM) has launched the Basic Services to the Urban Poor (BSUP) Programme to 
assist cities  and towns for taking up housing and infrastructural facilities for the urban 
poor in 63 selected cities  and the Integra ted Housing and Slum Development 
Programme (IIISDP) for taking up housing and slum upgradation programmes in non -
Mission  cities.  Both BSUP and IHSDP Schemes are under implementation since 
December. 2005. The Juration of JNNURM is seven years beginning from  the year 
2005-06. 
In so far as Andhra Pradesh is concerned, 16 projects under the BSUP programme 
and 26 projects under the IHSDP programme have been approved and which are at 
various stages of implementation. 
Apart from the above, the Andhra Pradesh Gover nment has reported that they have 
launched a programme titled  "iNDIRAMMA" for providing  pucca house for all 
eligible in a phased manner in three years from 2006-07 onwards. 
New rules for protection of wild tigers 
"62. SHRI R. S11UNMUGASUNDARAM: Will the PR IME MINISTER be pleased 
to  state  
(a) whether Government have made an \ request to ( hina for lifting the ban on 
trading   in tiger pails: 
(b) if so, the steps which are being taken to protect wild tiger  from depletion; 
(c) whether any attempt has been made to amend the existing rules in this regard; 
and 
(d) whether there is a proposal to frame new rules? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY  OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI  S. REGUPATHY): (a) No Sir. In fact. India has banned trade in the 
bod) parts (and their  derivatives) of tiger and other wild animals  included in Schedule 
I and Part II of Schedule II of the  Wildlife  (Protection)  Act, 1972. Hence. requesting 
China to lift the ban on trade in tiger parts does not arise. 
(b) The initiatives  taken by the Government of India  for conservation of wild 
animals including the tiger are given the Statement (See below). 
(c) and (d) The Wild Life Protection Act. I972 has been amended during 2006 to 
provide  enabling  provisions for creating  the National  Tiger Conservation Authority 
and the Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime Control Bureau, which have already 
been constituted for strengthening tiger conservation and protection of our wildlife.  
The penalties for offences relating  to tiger reserves have been made more stringent.  

Written Answers to [16 AUG.. 2007] Starred Questions       5 
Statement 
Steps taken by the Government to protect wild tiger from depletion Legal  
steps 
1. Amendment of the Wild Life (Protection) Act. 1972 for providing enabling 
provisions for constitution of the National Tiger Conservation Authority and  
the Tiger and Other Endangered Species Crime Control Bureau. The  
punishment in cases of offence within  a tiger reserve has been enhanced. The 
Act also provides for forfeiture of any equipment, vehicle  or weapon that ha s 
been used for committing any wild  life  offence. 
Administrative steps 
2. Strengthening of antipoaching  activities,  including  special  strategy for 
monsoon patrolling, by providing funding support to Tiger Reserve States, as 
proposed by them, for deployment of  antipoaching squads involving  ex-army 
personnel/home guards, apart from workforce comprising of local people, in 
addition to strengthening of communication/wireless facilities.  
3. Constitution of the National Tiger Conservation Authority with effect from 
4.09.2006, for strengthening tiger  conservation by, inter alia, ensuring 
normative standards in tiger reserve management, preparation of reserve specific 
tiger conservation plan,  laying  down annual audit report before Parliament, 
constituting  State  level  Stee ring Committees under the Chairmanship of 
Chief Ministers and establishment of Tiger Conservation Foundation. 
4. Constitution of a multidisciplinary  Tiger and Other  Endangered Species Crime 
Control Bureau (Wildlife Crime Control Bureau) with effect from 6.6. 2007 
comprising of officers from Police. Forest, Customs and other enforeement 
agencies to effectively control illegal  trade in wildlife.  
5. In principle approval accorded for declaring eight new Tiger Reserves 
Financial steps 
6. Financial and technical help is provided to the States  under various Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes, viz. Project Tiger and Development of National Parks and  
Sanctuaries for enhancing the capacity and infrastructure of the States  tor 
providing effective protection to wild animals. 
International Cooperation 
7. India  has a Memorandum of Understanding with  Nepal on controlling  
trans-boundary illegal trade in wildlife and conservation, apart from a protocol 
on tiger conservation with China. 
 
8. A Global Tiger Forum of Tiger Range Countries has been created  for 
addressing international issues related to tiger conservation. 
9. During the 14th meeting of the Conference of Parlies to CITES, which was held 
from 3rd to 15th June, 2007 at The Hague. India  introduced a resolution along  
with China. Nepal and the Russian Federation, which  contains  directions to 
Parties with operations breeding tigers on a commercial scale   tor restricting

such captive populations to a level supportive only  to conserving wild tigers. The 
resolution was adopted with minor amendments. Further, India made an 
intervention appealing to China to phase out tiger farming, and eliminate 
stockpiles of Asian big cats body parts and derivatives. The importance of 
continuing the ban on trade of body parts of tigers was emphasized. 
Venue crunch for wedding ceremonies 
*63. SHRIMATI HEMA MALINI: Will the Minister of URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that the Capital city is reeling under sev ere venue 
crunch during peak wedding season; 
(b) whether Government are also aware that people have started organising 
weddings on roads which causing trouble to residents in that area; 
(c) whether Government propose to appeal to the High Court to lift ban on farm  
houses and banquet halls to solemnise marriages; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT (SHRI S. JAIPAL REDDY): (a) The 
Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi (GNCTD) has reported that the 
facilities are inadequate during peak season. As per information received from local 
bodies, details regarding availability of authorised banquet halls, community centres, 
parks etc. for wedding ceremonies and other social functions in Delhi are given in the 
Statement (See below). 
(b) No permission is accorded for organising weddings on roads. 
(c) and (d) The High Court of Delhi vide order dated 17th February, 2006 directed 
that only in those farm houses where the metal road is 60 feet wide, weddings shall be 
permitted subject to meeting th e requirements of the draft guidelines with regard to 
parking space, noise pollution, sanitary conditions etc. The policy framed by GNCTD is 
under consideration before the High Court. The next date of hearing is 10.10.2007. The 
High Court imposed a ban on banquet halls in non -conforming areas and the ban is not 
applicable to banquet halls in conforming areas.

Missing of blank  passport booklets 
*65. SHRI MOTIUR RAHMAN: Will  the  Minister  of EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether thousands of blank passport booklets and vis a stickers were found 
missing from Missions and Posts abroad and if so, the details thereof: 
(b) whether a well -oiled racket, involving  the local police and passport offices 
issuing fake passports to foreign nationals from Afghanistan. Bangladesh. Pakistan and  
Sri Lanka exists:  
(c) if so, the details thereof: 
(d) the corrective measures taken to check malpractices and deficiencies in passport 
offices: and 
(e) the action taken against the officials responsible for issuing fake passports to 
foreign nationals and for loss of blank passport booklets and visa stickers? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE): (a) 
Some blank passport booklets and visa stickers supplied to a few Indian 
Missions/Posts abroad were not accounted for as mentioned in the Report of the 
Comptroller and Auditor General of India  on the Performance audit of Passport, Visa 
and Consular Services covering the period 2000- 01 to 2004-05. However, most of these 
documents were subsequently accounted for and details  are given in the Statement -I 
(See below). 
(b) and (c) While the Government have not come across am organised racket, a few 
cases have come to its notice, where Indian passports were issued by Passport Offices 
on the basis of forged documents to the nationals of Afghanistan. Pakistan and S ri Lanka 
and details are given in Statement-II (See below). 
(d) Government have taken several corrective measures to check malpractices and  
deficiencies in Passport Offices. These include  regular and surprise inspections,  
including  vigilance inspections of  Passport Offices, strengthening vigilance  
mechanisms in the Central Passport Organisation and ensuring greater accountability 
in the working of Passport Offices. Government have also initiated  steps to introduce  
biometric passports. 
(e) Government. have t aken action against errant officials  by sanctioning  
prosecution by the concerned agencies or through disciplinary proceedings, as  
required. Steps have also been taken to ensure the safety of documents during their  
movement from the India  Security Press, Nasik to end -users and for proper  
accountine of such documents.

Total reserves of thorium 
†443. SHRI SHREEGOPAL WAS: 
  SHRI BALAVANT ALIAS BAL APTE: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) the experiments carried out in the direction of producing atomic energy from  
thorium and the possibilities thereof; 
(b) the names of the States and the number of reserves found therein; 
(c) whether it is also available in the sea between India and Sri Lanka; 
(d) the efforts being made to preserve and utilize them; and 
(e) the percentage of atomic energy that could be met out of the total available 
reserves of thorium? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE PRIME MINISTER'S OFFICE (S HRI 
PRITHVIRAJ CHAVAN): (a) Thorium plays a pivotal role in Indian Nuclear power 
piogramme. Right from the inception of Indian nuclear power programme, work has 
been carried on all aspects of thorium utilisation viz., mining and extraction, fuel 
fabrication, irradiation in reactors, reprocessing, re- fabrication and setting up of reactors 
using fissile uranium derived from Thorium. Studies are also underway for utilisation of 
thorium in different types of reactors. 
Thorium fuel fabrication through powder pel let route has been well established. Few 
tons of fuel has been made for CIRUS and Dhruva, for PHWR and for blanket 
assemblies for FBTR. Few pins have been fabricated using mixed oxides of (Th -Pu) for 
irradiation in research reactors. 
Thoria bundles have be en used in the initial cores of PHWR. The irradiation 
experience of thoria fuel in CIRUS, Dhruva, PHWRs and test irradiations is 
satisfactory. 
The thoria pins of CIRUS have been reprocessed to obtain U233. The recovered 
U233 has been used as fuel for critical facilities at Trombay and for K.AMINI reactor at 
Kalpakkam. The Post Irradiation Examination of the thoria bundle irradiated in PHWR 
has also been carried out for validation of theoretical analyses. 
Studies have been carried out regarding use of thoriu m in different types of reactors 
with respect to fuel management, reactor control and fuel utilisation. 
To, accelerate thorium utilisation, BARC has designed a 300 MWe Advanced Heavy 
Water Reactor (AHWR). This reactor will demonstrate various aspects of th orium fuel 
technology. The AHWR was included as a case study in IAEA's INPRO project on 
innovative reactor and fuel cycles.

Guidelines for disposal of e-waste  
479. SHRI B.J. PANDA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that around 150,000 tonnes of electronic waste is generated in 
India, while the guidelines for disposal of this waste are yet to be finalized; 
(b) whether Delhi, Mumbai and, other big cities are burdened with e -waste that is 
too dangerous to be handled in congested areas and this menace is growing consistently; 
and 
(c) if so. the action plan of Government to address this issue? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (c) Based on a survey conducted 
under the guidance of the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB), it has been 
estimated that about 1,46,000 tonnes of waste from Electrical and Electronic Equipment 
(WEEE) is generated annually in the country. Delhi, Mumbai and other big cities have 
been identified as major e- waste generating areas in the country. In order to address the 
problem of e -waste, the Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) got a study on the. 
assessment of electrical and electronic waste generation conducted. They have also 
undertaken the task of preparation of "Guidelines for Environmentally Sound 
Management of 2 -Waste" for the State Pollution Control Boards and Pollution Control 
Committee in Union Territories. In this connection, the Ministry of Environment and 
Forests in the  Government of India has constituted a Task Force comprising of 
representatives of the concerned Ministries and experts for finalization of these 
guidelines. 
The Ministry of Environment and Forests have also notified the Hazardous Waste 
(Management and Handling) Rules, 1989 as amended in 2000 and 2003 which regulate 
the generation, collection, storage, treatment, disposal as well as export and import of 
hazardous wastes. The provisions under the Hazardous Wastes (Management and 
Handling) Rules, 1989 as amen ded in 2000 and 2003 include e -waste. The processes 
generating hazardous wastes are listed in Schedule 1 of these rules. The residues and 
wastes generated from the operations in electronic industry are already considered as 
hazardous wastes and are included at s. No. 31 of Schedule 1 of these rules. Further, the 
import and export of e -waste is also regulated under Schedule 3 of these rules. As per 
the provisions of these rules, the import of e -waste is regulated under Schedule 3 of 
these rules wherein Elect rical and Electronic Assemblies are covered under category A 
1180 in the list A and B 1110 in list B of the Schedule 3. The import of such waste is 
permitted only for direct reuse and not for recycling or final disposal.

state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of  the U.N. Environment Programme (UNEP) 
pushing for a global phase out of mercury: 
(b) the reasons for Government promoting the use of CFLs, which contain mercury 
and is a serious health hazard and cause catastrophe to the environment; 
(c) whether Government have no functioning recycling scheme, and on account of 
this most of the mercury would be released in the air; 
(d) whether CFI s' not only reduce bills,  they also keep the overall power demand 
low; and 
(e) the steps being taken to check the flow, dumping and flooding of Indian market

Programme (UNEP), Governing Council in its  24th Session held in Nairobi in 
February, 2007 adopted the decision LNEP/GC/24/3 on "Chemicals" and concluded that 
further long term international action is required to reduce risks to human health and 
environment and that, for this reason, the options of enhanced voluntary measures and 
new or existing international legal instruments will be review ed and assessed in order to 
make progress in addressing this issue. The Governing Council decided to establish an 
Adhoe Joint Working Group of Governments, regional economic integration 
organizations and stakeholder representatives and requested the Execut ive Director to 
present a report on progress in the implementation of the present decision to the 
Governing Council at its twenty-fifth session. 
(b) As per the Bureau or Energy Efficiency (BEE), Ministry of Power. Compact 
Fluorescent Lamps (CFLs) have potential to save energy and thereby reduce green house 
gas emissions that contribute to global climate change. Mercury is essential component 
of CFLs. The amount of mercury in them ranges from 1.3 milligram < 5 milligram 
which does not pose health hazard to humans. No mercury is released when the bulbs 
are intact or in use. Unregulated disposal of CFLs can create environmental impacts.

75% less energy than incandescent bulbs, reduce electricity bills of consumers

Under Rule 5 of the Customs Tariff (Identification, Assessment and Collection of 
Anti-Dumping Duty on Dumped Articles and for Determi nation of Injury) Rules, 1995, 
anti-dumping investigations are initiated by Designated Authority after examining the

Reducing high level of mercury containment 
484 SHRI ABU AS1M AZMI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that high levels of mercury is found in the air and most 
particularly in hospitals which threatens the health of patients and medical.staff; 
(b) whether it is also a fact that USA has come forward to help our country to re duce 
such high levels of mercury containment; and 
 (c) if so. the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) The  Bio -Medical Waste 
(Management and Handling) Rules, 1998 and the subsequen t amendments thereof, do 
not prescribe any emission limits for mercury from bio -medical waste incinerators. The 
National Ambient Air Quality Standards (NAAQS) notified under the Environment 
(Protection) Act, 1986 for various areas including sensitive areas  like hospitals, also do 
not cover mercury. 
Improper handling and accidental breakage of instruments containing mercury  
can cause pollution.         
The Central Pollution Control Board (CPCB) has requested all State  Pollution 
ControJ Boards (SPCBs)/Poliution Control Committees (PPCs) of Union Territories that 
mercury spillage/losses in healthcare facilities need to be given proper attention not only 
in respect of collection of the spilled mercury, its storage \and sending the same back to 
the manufacturers, but also for taking all necessary measures to ensure that the spilled 
waste generated from the healthcare facilities is taken care for its proper disposal. 
Further, the Schedule -II of Hazardous Waste (Management and Handling) Rules, 2003 
provides that any waste containing equal to or greater than 50 ppm of mercury in it is a 
hazardous waste and the concerned generators of such Waste. including healthcare 
facilities, are required to dispose the same as per the Hazardous Waste (Management 
and Handling) Rules, 2003. 
No ill effects of mercury in any Central Government Hospitals have come to the 
notice of the Government.

Protection of river Ganga 
485. SHRI ABU ASIM AZMI: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state:  
(a) whether Government are aware that River Ganga is among the ten rivers in the 
world which are going to be dried up in the nearest future; 
(b) if so, the action which is proposed to be taken by Government for the protection 
of River Ganga and to protect the fertility of the land for proper agricultural production;  
(c) whether other rivers in the country are also affected in this regard; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) to (d) In a report entitled' "World's 
top 10 rivers at risk", the WWF, an International Non -Governmental Organisation 
(NGO), has listed the river Ganga as one of the World's ten rivers facing risk. The 
Central Government is not aware of the data -base and the methodology adapted by the 
said NGO for making this Report. The report profiles the biodiversity of river Ganga, 
and perceives over extraction of water for agriculture and excessive water diversions 
affecting natural flows as major threats to the river. The Report does not consider other 
Indian rivers as facing danger of getting dried up. 
The flows of river Ganga are being monitored by Central Water Commission (CWC) 
under the Ministry of Water Resources at various places on regular basis. The last point 
is Farakka Barrage after which the river enters into Bangladesh. As per the flows 
measured during the lean season (1st January to 31st May) at Farakka Barrage, the flows 
of the last five years are quite comparable with the long term flows (1949 -88). There is 
no apparent reduction in the available water in river Ganga at this terminal point even 
during the critical season. The CWC pursues an approach for integrated and coordinated 
development of surface and groundwater resources and their conjunctive use. The CWC 
has formulated a National Perspective Plan for water resources development in the 
country that envisages inter-linking of rivers for transfer of water from surplus basins to 
water deficit basins for optimum utilization of water in the country. Under the Centrally 
Sponsored Scheme of National River Conservation Plan of the Ministry of Environment 
and Forests, various works  are undertaken for pollution abatement in major rivers 
including Ganga through interception and diversion of sewage for its treatment and 
construction of Sewage

treatment Plants and Low Cost Sa nitation. Under the Ganga Action Plan -(GAP) Phase 1 
& II, 1747 mld. (million litres per day) of sewage treatment capacity has been created  so 
far. With the pollution  abatement works completed so far under Ganga Action  Plan, 
the water quality  of the river G anga has shown discernible improvement at major 
locations over its  pre-GAP quality as per the water quality monitoring undertaken by 
independent reputed institutions in the country. The National Environment Policy. 2006 
also  advocates an integrated approach for management of river basins by the concerned 
river authorities, ensuring maintenance of adequate flows, adherence to water quality  
standards throughout their course in all seasons and protection of land resources.

Melting of Himalayan Glaciers 
491. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether i t is a fact that UN Inter -Governmental Panel on Climate Change has 
warned that the Himalayan Glaciers are melting, with dire long -term consequences for 
water in the North; 
(b) if so, whether Government have made any study on northern glaciers and their 
environment impact likely to occur, for the northern regions; 
(c) whether Government have any knowledge about the melting of Himalayan 
glaciers and at what pace they are melting; and 
(d) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT A ND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Geological Survey of India (GSI) has been undertaking glaciological studies 
on Himalayan glaciers, since 1906 and systematic glaciological monitoring is being 
carried out in the Northern region since 1 974. GSI has monitored more than 35 glaciers 
so far. During the last five years, alone, it has monitored 12 glaciers in Ghaghra basin in 
Uttarakhand and Bears, Parvati, Ravi and Bhaga basins in Himachal Pradesh. GSI has not 
undertaken any study to correlat e the river discharge, water level changes in sea and 
ocean and the recession of the glaciers. In addition to glaciers, seasonal snow cover, 
groundwater, rainfall etc. contribute to the river discharge. Due to enhanced melting of 
ice, consequent upon faster recession, the runoff of the Himalayan rivers may increase 
marginally. 
(c) and (d) GSI is aware of the melting of the Himalayan glaciers. Compilations of 
the data on secular movement of glaciers have revealed that the majority of the glaciers 
of the Himalayan region are passing through a phase of recession, which is a worldwide 
phenomenon. No abnormal rate of recession has been reported by GSI. Even in the 
Himalayan region, the rate of recession in different climatic zones is found to be variable 
on average and in year to year basis. The retreat parameters of 35 glaciers show that 43% 
of the glaciers in the Himalayan region are retreating in the range of 10 to 20m/yr. The 
causative factors for this variable retreat may be subnormal snowfall, higher temperature  
during summer, less severe winter or a combination of all of them. It could also be 
attributed to the phenomenon of rise in temperature, global warming, a topic which is 
still under debate.

Written Answers to [16 AUG., 2007] Unstarred Questions    11 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF ENVIRONMENT AND 
FORESTS (SHRI NAMO NARAIN MEENA): (a) A meeting of the Inter- Governmental 
Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) was held in Bangkok during April 30 - May 4. 2007 
to consider and adopt a report of the Working Group III of the IPCC on mitigation of 
climate change. The IPCC is a specialised scientific body and is charged with the 
responsibility for preparation of scientific assessment based on the peer reviewed 
published literature. it is not a forum to develop consensus on the actions to be taken by 
the various countries. The report of the IPCC on mitigation of climate change adopted 
on M ay 4, 2007 at Bangkok. Thailand provides global level assessment of new 
literature on scientific, technological, environmental, economic and social aspect of 
climate change, after the year 2002. Further, the report provides global trends of 
greenhouse gas emission; mitigation in short and medium term (until 2030); mitigation 
in long term (after 2030); policies, measures and instruments to mitigate climate 
change: sustainable development and climate change mitigation and gaps in knowledge.  
(b) and (c) No suc h consensus was reached on any target of 2 degree celcius for the 
global warming. However, the Government of India  is a Party to Kyoto Protocol to the 
United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) and has set up 
the National Clean Developm ent Mechanism Authority to accord Host Country 
Approvals to eligible  Clean Development Mechanism (CDM) projects as per the 
requirements of Marrakesh Accords Although India as a developing country does not 
have any mitigation commitments. India  also has the largest number of projects under 
CDM of the Kyoto Protocol. which reduce net emissions of greenhouse gases. Further, 
the message of CDM has been propagated through various workshops and seminars 
organized from time to time. Capacity building programmes ha ve been undertaken for 
various stakeholders with multilateral and bilateral agencies. 
A sustainable development path is being followed in India  by a range of policies 
and programmes to mitigate  climate change: 
(a) ensuring energy conservation and improved energy efficiency in various 
sectors as well as setting up of Bureau of Energy Efficiency; 
(b) promoting use of renewable energy: 
(c) power sector reforms and active renewable energy programme: 
(d) use of cleaner and lesser carbon intensive fuel for  transport 
(e) fuel switch ing  to cleaner energy: 
(f) afforestation and conservation of forests; 
(g) promotion of clean coal technologies: 
(h)    reduction of gas flaring; 
(i)     encouraging Mass Rapid Transport systems: and 
(j)     environmental quality management for all sectors.

State Governments concerned and it is for them to take appropriate action.

Abhiyan to strengthen the elected women of the PRIs under the aegis of the "Chalo Gaon 
Ki Ore" rubric of the National Commission for Women. A core group comprising selected 
EWRs, activists, academics etc. is nominated by the State Government/ Government of 
India  to draft and facilitate a draft women's charter for the EWRs of the state stating 
thereon t heir particular issues.  Subsequently, all women Zila Pramukhs, all women 
Pradhans and selected women Sarpanchs from each district of the state, as well as Core 
Group members and some eminent personalities are invited to a said two day conference 
of panchayat women. A women's charter comprising all the major points distilled  from 
the discussions with the women representatives of the PRIs is then finalized.  
Most EWRs see themselves as isolated and unorganized, functioning without the 
support of a structure and have spoken of the need to form into groups or associations so 
as to be part of a forum that addresses their special needs in a largely male -dominated 
social and political milieu. The Panchayat Mahila Shakti Abhiyan has been

Decline in poverty 
533. SHRIMATI SUPRIYA SULE: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the number of poor Indians declined by 4.3 per cent in the five years 
from March 2000, but there are still  24 crore people living in acute want in an economy 
that has grown at nearly 8 per cent over the period; 
(b) whether the National Sample Survey report also reveals that the decline in 
poverty was comparatively much steep in rural areas where the percentage of people 
living  below poverty line fell to 21.8 per cent in 2004-05 from 27.1 per cent; and 
(c) the steps Government propose to take for removing the poverty in India? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI M.V. 
RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The Planning Commission estimates the incidence of poverty 
at national and state level from the large sample survey on household consumer 
expenditure conducted by the National Sample Survey Organization (NSSO) at an 
interval of approximately five years following the methodology contained in the Report 
of the Expert G roup on Estimation of Proportion and Number of Poor (Lakadwala 
Committee). Based on this, the poverty ratio (i.e., the percentage of people living below 
the poverty line) has been estimated for the years 1999-2000 and 2004-05 using the NSS 
consumer expenditure data of the 55th and 61st Rounds respectively. The poverty ratio 
in 1999- 2000 is estimated as 26.1 per cent for the country as a whole, i.e., rural and 
urban areas taken together. The corresponding poverty ratio in 2004 -05, based on MRP 
consumption di stribution (Mixed Recall Period consumption in which the consumer 
expenditure data for five non -food items, namely, clothing, footwear, durable  goods, 
education and institutional medical expenses are collected from 365 -day recall period 
and the consumption data for the remaining items are collected from 30 -day recall 
period), is estimated as 21.8 per cent. Therefore, the poverty ratio declined by 4.3 
percentage points between 1999-2000 and 

108   Written Answers to [RAJYA SABHA] Unstarred Questions 
2004-05.  The  number of poor on this  basis  is estimated  as 23.85  crore  in 2004- 05. 
(b) The poverty ratio in the rural areas fell to 21.8 per cent in 2004-05 from 27.1 per 
cent in 1999-2000 as compared to 21.7 per cent in 2004- 05 from 23.6 per cent in 1999-
2000 in the urban areas. 
(c) The Government has adopted a three pronged strategy for reducing poverty: (i) 
acceleration of economic growth with a focus on sectors which are employment 
intensive; (ii) human and social development through provision of basic minimum 
services; and (iii)  direct attack on poverty through employment and income generating 
programmes and asset building for the poor. A number of programmes/ schemes have 
been introduced by the Government from time to time to improve the conditions of the 
poor people living  below the poverty line in rural and urban areas.

536. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that several irrigation projects have been hampered due  
to financial crunch and various irrigation projects are pending for approvals; 
(b) if so, Government's response there to and the steps taken so far by the Union 
Government for early completion of all  the ongoing irrigation projects; 
(c) Wether Government have explored the possibilities for increasing the irrigation 
capacity in the coming years  keeping in view the irrigation demand in the country; and  
(d) if so, the details of initiatives formulated by Government to meet the demand? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING (SHRI M.V. 
RAJASEKHARAN): (a) The respon sibility of planning, funding and execution of 
irrigation projects primarily lies with the State Government concerned as irrigation is a 
State Subject. The priority for irrigation sector funding has declined from about 22.54% 
in first Plan to about 6.28% in Tenth Plan. Also States take up large number of irrigation 
projects and the resources are invariably thin spread. 
Irrigation and Flood Control projects, which are located on inter-state rivers and 
tributaries, are being techno-economically appraised by Central Water Commission. The 
projects are further being considered in Advisory Committee for Irrigation, Flood . 
Control and Multipurpose projects of Ministry of Water Resources for acceptance and 
according investment approval by Planning Commission. 
(b) to (d) The guidelines for the Accelerated Irrigation Benefit Programme 
have been relaxed in December 2006 and assistance is provided to the states in the  
form of either 90 per cent grant or 25 per cent grant for completing the irrigation  
projects. 
Under Bha rat Nirman, 10 million  hectare is proposed to be brought under 
irrigation during the four -year period 2005- 2009. The Working Group on Water 
Resources for the Eleventh Five -Year Plan has suggested a target of creating 16 million 
hectare of irrigation potential. The State Governments have to provide adequate funds 
under the State Plan for achieving these targets'.

540. SHRI. KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of SHIPPING,  
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government would direct the Capital Transport Department that Zonal 
Transport Departments should not be more than five kilometres distance from the areas 
it would cover in order to decongest the existing transport departments; 
(b) if so. by when i t is expected to be done in order to facilitate ladies and senior 
citizens; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER Of STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIYAPPA): (a) to (c) Road Transport 
is a State subject. It is the prerogative of the State Governments to open zonal offices of 
the Transport Department keeping in view the number of motor vehicles, requirement of 
its citizens and importance of the area/zone due to social, economic and geographical 
reasons. T here is no such proposal on the part of this department to direct the State 
Governments to open more zonal offices.

Four-laning of NH 215 
543. MS. PRAM1LA BOHIDAR: 
SHRI B.J. PANDA: 
Will the Minister of SHIPPING ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether the four-laning of the Panikoili-Rajamunda NH-215, connecting iron ore 
rich Keonjhar to Kalinga Nagar Industrial Complex in Jajpur, is likely to be delayed; 
(b) if so, the details with reasons therefor; 
(c) whether the above stretch of r oad is accident prone area due to traffic congestion 
and the residents of Jajpur and Keonjhar have been demanding immediate four -laning of 
the NH for safety of life and property; and 
(d) if so, the action plan of the Centre to expedite its completion bn a top -priority 
basis? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K..H. MUNIYAPPA): (a) to (c) Keeping in view 
the increase in traffic and consequential congestion coupled with public demand, the 
four-laning NH 215 from P anikoili-Rajamunda has been included under the National 
Highway Development Programme (NHDP) Phase -IIIA of National Highway Authority 
of India (NHAI). NHAI has already taken up the work of preparation of Detailed Project 
Report (DPR) and the bids on Build  Operate and Transfer (BOT) basis will be invited 
after the necessary approval from Public Private Partnership Appraisal Committee (PPP 
AC). 
(d) The tentative target date of completion of four -laning of NH 215 is December, 
2010.

Housing under Master Plan-2021 
585. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Master Plan -2021 has focussed on housing the rich and 
the economically weaker sections of society, ignoring the middle class; 
(b) whether there is any lack of vital resources like power and water; and 
(c) the reaction of Government thereon? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN DEVELOPMENT 
(SHRI AJAY MAKEN): (a) The Master Pl an for Delhi -2021 aims to ensure housing 
and shelter options for all categories of people. The proposed housing strategy 
incorporates specific approaches for development of new housing areas, upgradation 
and re-densification of existing housing areas including unauthorised colonies, housing 
in villages and Special Area. The housing strategy recommends four categories of 
Dwelling Units (DU) sizes with different density norms. Keeping in view the socio -
economic composition of the population, around 50- 55% of the housing requirement 
would be for urban poor and the economically weaker sections in the form of house of 
two rooms or less with average plinth area of about 25 square metres to 40 square 
metres. 
The four categories are as follows:- 
Slum/EWS housing (upto 30 sq.m) —       600 DUs/ha  
Category I (above 30 - upto 40 sq.m) —       500 DUs/ha  
Category II (above 40 - upto 80 sq.m) —       250 DUs/ha  
Category III (above 80 sq.m) 175 DUs/ha

The average plinth area per house to be achieved in various neighbourhoods will also 
depend on composition of various income groups to be accommodated in the composite 
housing schemes. The housing strategy aims to harness the potential of the public, 
private/Corporate and household sectors. 
(b) and (c) MPD -2021 has projected the total requirement of resources like power  
and water for the year 2021 and has also recommended the strategies for physical  
infrastructure development. Delhi Jal Board has initiated various step s to augment  
water supply and to take care of the requirement of water for the projected population  
of the city in 2011 and 2021. With regard to power, according to the perspective plan,  
the Delhi Transco Ltd. has estimated the requirement of power in Delh i in the year  
2021 as 11,000 MW. The Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi has  
initiated various measures for augmentation of the power supply.
